sections.title: Explanation
sections.body:
> **In one line:** A consistency model is the contract a distributed data store makes about which values a read may return given the history of writes that preceded it — ranging from **linearizability** (reads see the latest write as if there were a single copy) through **sequential**, **causal**, and **read-your-writes** down to **eventual consistency** (replicas converge only after writes stop).

A consistency model is the small print on a distributed data store. It tells you, given a sequence of writes spread across replicas, which values a read is allowed to return — and therefore which application invariants you can rely on without writing extra coordination code. The strongest model, **linearizability** (Herlihy and Wing, 1990), makes the system appear as a single piece of memory: every read returns the value written by the most recent write before it, in real time, and concurrent operations appear in some total order that respects real-time precedence. Achieving linearizability requires consensus on every write and usually a quorum read, which is why Google Spanner uses TrueTime plus Paxos groups and pays a ~5–7ms commit wait. **Sequential consistency** (Lamport, 1979) drops the real-time requirement: there exists a single total order of all operations that every client agrees on, but that order need not match wall-clock order. A read can return a stale value as long as every client sees the same sequence of values. This is the model of a single-primary SQL database with asynchronous replication: it is sequentially consistent within itself, even if replicas lag.

**Causal consistency** preserves *happens-before* relationships (Lamport, 1978): if write A causally precedes write B (B was sent by a client that saw A, or B's reply was sent after A's reply), then any client that sees B must also see A. Concurrent writes can appear in any order, so two clients may see them differently. Causal consistency is the strongest model that does not require consensus and is therefore achievable with availability under partitions — COPS, Bolt-on Causal Consistency, and MongoDB's causal sessions implement it. **Read-your-writes** (session consistency) guarantees that a client never sees its own writes disappear: once you write X=1, every subsequent read you do returns 1 or a later value, never the older 0. Amazon DynamoDB achieves this with session-sticky node routing plus write-ack forwarding. **Monotonic reads** guarantees that once a client sees a value, it never sees an older one — important for caches and feed readers where regression would be confusing. **Monotonic writes** guarantees a client's writes are seen in the order it issued them.

At the bottom sits **eventual consistency**: given no new writes, all replicas eventually converge to the same value, but during convergence a read may return any value the replica has ever seen. Amazon DynamoDB's eventual reads mode, Cassandra at consistency `ONE`, and DNS all sit here. The trade-off across the spectrum is mechanical: stronger models need more cross-replica coordination (more round trips, more quorum members, more conflict resolution), which raises latency and reduces availability during partitions. Weaker models let each replica answer locally in sub-millisecond time but push correctness burden to the application, which must reason about staleness, idempotency, and conflict resolution. Real systems rarely sit at a single point — Spanner is linearizable for writes but offers stale reads; Cassandra lets you set consistency per query; DynamoDB offers both `consistentRead=true` and `consistentRead=false` on the same table.

Real-world systems illustrate the spectrum. **Google Spanner** is linearizable globally, achieved by TrueTime-bounded commit wait plus Paxos per shard, and is the substrate for AdWords billing and Google Play — workloads where charging the wrong amount is unacceptable. **MongoDB** offers causal consistency sessions so a client that writes a document and then queries for it sees its own write, even when reads are routed to secondary replicas. **Cassandra** is tunable from `ANY` (write accepted by any node, even a hinted handoff) through `ONE`, `QUORUM`, `LOCAL_QUORUM`, up to `ALL`, letting each query pay for exactly the consistency it needs. **Amazon DynamoDB** exposes `consistentRead=true` for ~2x the read-unit cost when you need strong reads. **etcd and ZooKeeper** are linearizable for writes via Raft/Zab, and offer linearizable reads through a quorum round or a leader-lease optimization. **Redis Cluster** is sequentially consistent within a slot but offers no cross-slot transactional guarantees.

The architect's job is to pick the *weakest* model that still preserves the application's invariants. Inventory and billing need linearizability — you cannot oversell the last concert ticket to two people. Profile photos, comment counts, recommendation feeds, and "people you may know" need only eventual consistency, and choosing stronger would waste money on consensus for no business value. Session consistency is the sweet spot for user-facing apps where a user must always see their own writes but other users' staleness is invisible. Causal consistency shines for collaborative editing and chat threads, where reply chains must respect causality but global ordering is overkill. Getting this choice right is often the difference between a service that scales linearly by adding nodes and one that bottoms out at the throughput of a single consensus leader. A useful mental model: every step down the consistency ladder roughly halves coordination cost and doubles achievable throughput — but adds a new class of bugs you must reason about in the application layer.

### Mermaid Diagram ```mermaid flowchart LR A[Linearizability
real-time total order] --> B[Sequential
total order, no real-time] B --> C[Causal
respects happens-before] C --> D[Read-your-writes
session sticky] D --> E[Eventual
converges when writes stop] style A fill:#fdd,stroke:#c00 style E fill:#dfd,stroke:#0a0 ``` ### ASCII Diagram ``` stronger weaker ----------------------------------------------------------------- Linearizable > Sequential > Causal > RYW / Monotonic > Eventual ----------------------------------------------------------------- consensus? yes yes no no no RTT cost 2-3x 1-2x 1x 0 0 available no (CP) no (CP) yes yes yes (AP) examples Spanner PG/MySQL COPS DynamoDB sess Cassandra ONE ``` ### Walkthrough 1. A write arrives at the leader; under linearizability the leader must commit via consensus before replying. 2. A read at the highest consistency level goes through the same quorum round-trip — slow but always fresh. 3. Stepping down to causal consistency, the read can be served from any replica whose vector clock is a superset of the client's session vector. 4. At eventual consistency the read returns whatever the local replica currently holds — possibly stale. 5. When writes stop, anti-entropy (read-repair, hint handoff, Merkle-tree sync) converges all replicas.

sections.title: Code
sections.body:
```python
# Mock store showing linearizable vs eventual reads on the same data.
import threading, time

class Replica:
    def __init__(self, name):
        self.name = name
        self.value = 0
        self.version = 0
        self.lock = threading.Lock()

class KVStore:
    def __init__(self, replica_names):
        self.replicas = [Replica(n) for n in replica_names]
        self.leader = self.replicas[0]

    def write_linearizable(self, v):
        # CP: leader commits to a quorum before acking the client.
        acks = 1                                   # leader counts
        for r in self.replicas[1:]:
            with r.lock:
                if r.version < self.leader.version + 1:
                    r.value, r.version = v, self.leader.version + 1
                    acks += 1
        if acks * 2 <= len(self.replicas):         # quorum check
            raise RuntimeError("no quorum, write refused")
        with self.leader.lock:
            self.leader.value, self.leader.version = v, self.leader.version + 1

    def read_linearizable(self):
        # Quorum read: return the highest-version value seen.
        best = (self.leader.value, self.leader.version)
        for r in self.replicas[1:]:
            with r.lock:
                if r.version > best[1]:
                    best = (r.value, r.version)
        return best[0]

    def write_eventual(self, v):
        # AP: leader acks immediately; replicas lag and converge later.
        with self.leader.lock:
            self.leader.value, self.leader.version = v, self.leader.version + 1
        threading.Thread(target=self._propagate, args=(v,)).start()

    def _propagate(self, v):
        time.sleep(0.05)                           # simulate replication lag
        for r in self.replicas[1:]:
            with r.lock:
                if r.version < self.leader.version:
                    r.value, r.version = v, self.leader.version

    def read_eventual(self, replica_idx=1):
        with self.replicas[replica_idx].lock:
            return self.replicas[replica_idx].value

store = KVStore(["A", "B", "C"])
store.write_linearizable(10)
print("linearizable read:", store.read_linearizable())   # 10
store.write_eventual(20)
print("eventual read (B, immediately):", store.read_eventual(1))  # may be 10
time.sleep(0.2)
print("eventual read (B, after convergence):", store.read_eventual(1))  # 20
```

quiz.question: What is the difference between sequential consistency and linearizability? Give a concrete example where they diverge.
options: Stale-read budgeting is the practice of explicitly deciding, per feature, the maximum staleness a user can tolerate, then choosing the cheapest consistency level that meets the budget.

quiz.explanation: Sequential consistency requires that there exists a single total order of all operations such that each client's program order is preserved and each read returns the value written by the most recent write in that total order; it does not require that this total order respect real-time ordering between clients.

quiz.question: What does causal consistency preserve, and why is it the strongest model available under partitions?
options: Stale-read budgeting is the practice of explicitly deciding, per feature, the maximum staleness a user can tolerate, then choosing the cheapest consistency level that meets the budget.
Linearizability is the guarantee that every operation appears to take effect atomically at a single point in real time between the operation's invocation and its response, so concurrent…

quiz.explanation: Causal consistency preserves the happens-before relation (Lamport, 1978): if operation A causally precedes operation B — because B's issuing client saw the result of A, or B was issued by the same client after A, or there is a chain of such dependencies — then any client that observes B must also observe A. Concurrent operations (those with no causal relationship) can be seen in different orders by different clients.

The two messages are concurrent (no causal relationship) so causal consistency is the natural fit.

quiz.explanation: Read-your-writes guarantees that a client never reads a value older than what it wrote — if you wrote X=5, subsequent reads return 5 or a later value. Monotonic reads guarantees that a client never sees time go backwards — once you read X=5, you never again read X=3. Monotonic writes guarantees that a client's own writes are seen by all observers in the order it issued them.

quiz.explanation: Cassandra lets you set the consistency level on every query — ANY, ONE, LOCAL_ONE, QUORUM, LOCAL_QUORUM, ALL — so each call pays for exactly the durability and freshness it needs. Choosing QUORUM means the coordinator waits for acknowledgements from a majority of replicas for that key (with replication factor RF=3, that is 2 of 3).
